Barcode Encoding

AlgorithmsCountingParity
Game: Explore how a product code turns into the black and white bars a scanner reads.
How to play: Change the highlighted digit with the arrows or the + and − buttons, switch between the two code types, or make a new code. The bars and the note below them say what changed.

Code:

Look for the math

A barcode looks like a random picket fence, but every digit is written with the same seven equal bars. The pattern is chosen so that a scanner only has to measure how long each black and white stretch is.

Seven bars, four stretches

Each digit uses seven bars, written below as 1 for black and 0 for white. Adjacent bars of the same colour merge into one wide stretch, called a generalized bar. Every digit becomes exactly four stretches that alternate colour. For example, the left-side code for 0 is 0001101: white 3, black 2, white 1, black 1. We checked all ten digits: every one of them has four stretches, and none is wider than four single bars, just as the cut-the-knot page says.

Odd, even and mirror

Write a digit's left-side bars and flip every colour: white becomes black and black becomes white. That is the right-side code, used for the last six digits of a UPC-A UPC-A code. Flip it back end-to-end and you get the left-side code with parity called even. All left-side codes end in a black bar; all right-side codes end in a space. Those two facts and the four-stretch rule were verified for all ten digits.

The first digit that has no bars

In an EAN-13 EAN-13 code, the first digit is not drawn at all. It is a key into a table of six parities: a 1 means use the odd code and a 0 means use the even code. So 4 selects odd, odd, even, odd, even, even. We compared the whole table with the one printed on the page and found the same ten rows. Putting a 0 in front of a UPC-A code makes its left six digits all odd, so the bars are identical to UPC-A; we checked this on 200 randomly generated codes.

Guards and a final check

Every code opens and closes with the same three bars, black-white-black (101), and both halves meet at white-black-white-black-white (01010). That is 3 + 42 + 5 + 42 + 3 = 95 bars in total. The page also notes that barcodes date from 1973; that is history, not something a logic test can check. The last digit of a real code is a check digit, worked out from the others; the "New code" button uses that rule so every example it makes is valid.

Try setting the EAN-13 system digit to 0 and then to 4: watch which half of the bars changes, and which half stays put.
